synopsis: Grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to deceleration itself; in the New South Wales example, a 100 t rigid truck designed for a 20% grade and tested on 9% requires 1.79 m/s² deceleration, with about 1.04 m/s² attributable to grade correction alone [f145, f5900, f5901, f5902]. NIOSH reports retarder disadvantage at excessive speed on descents steeper than 9%, and a stopping model found combinations where downhill grade exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop [f3085, f5903]. Automatic braking can itself create instability and other secondary hazards on grades, supporting context-dependent intervention rather than a universal brake command; Komatsu documentation accessed in 2026 tells wheel-loader users to disable stop control on steep slopes and in several other hazardous operating conditions [f1129, f1975, f10550]. Published validation of simulated heavy-machine stopping distances on slopes and difficult surfaces was not found, while the cited MOSH closed-loop testing is restricted to unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less and does not cover slope and loaded cases [f253, f3743, f3970, f5564, f5565]. The booklet therefore recommends retaining physical stopping tests across machine classes, load, slope and surface extremes, and documenting the grades and environmental ranges for which validation is valid rather than assuming a model conservative on dry soil remains conservative on an icy grade [f7881, f8009, f7965].
